text.p: Tatneft, Russia's fourth biggest oil producer, must cut costs and acquire downstream assets if it is to prosper and not just ride on its reputation as a recently successful independent, oil analysts said on Thursday.

A company spokesman said Tatneft's annual general meeting, set for Friday at company headquarters in the semi-autonomous republic of Tatarstan, would focus on strategic plans for the future as well as 1996 results.
"The three main things that will be discussed are voting on a new board, changes to the charter and voting on dividend payments," the spokesman said.
Analysts see Tatneft's long-term future in linking up with refineries and driving down high production costs.
"Tatneft should not just remain an upstream operation," said Ivan Mazalov, oil and gas analyst at CentreInvest Securities in Moscow. "If they do that, then they're done for."
AO Tatneft produced 23.70 million tonnes (474,000 barrels per day) of crude oil in 1996, down two percent from 24.14 million tonnes (482,800 bpd) in 1995.
The levels are far below its dizzying success in 1975, when the discovery of new fields sent output gushing to a peak 103.7 million tonnes (2.7 million bpd).
Production in 1997 is widely expected to remain stable on 1996 or even edge up slightly.

"The company produced 5.7 million tonnes of oil in the first quarter 1997 -- well in line with 1997 projected production levels of 25 million tonnes and boding well for a third year of stable output levels," brokerage Renaissance Capital said in a report.

But with no refining capacity of its own, Tatneft risks being squeezed out by Russia's vertically-integrated oil firms, which are rushing to snap up the best of a generally bad bunch of refineries in a drive to boost products output.
Mazalov said Tatneft might wish to eye Ukraine's Kremenchug refinery, since it is linked by pipeline to Tatarstan.
Tatneft was the first Russian oil comapny to reverse the steep output declines which plagued the sector in the late 1980s and early 1990s and are still a problem for many of its competitors.
But upstream, a high proportion of Tatneft's oil deposits are expensive to tap, and only tax concessions from regional authorities have allowed it to produce profitably.

But costs could fall long term, since Tatneft's key Romanshkinskoye oil field was now on a list of seven mineral and hydrocarbon reserves which recently qualified for development on a production-sharing basis.
"It is a good thing for Tatneft that their biggest field -- the Romanshkinskoye deposit -- was on the list," said one Western oil analyst based in Moscow.
The lower house of parliament approved the list earlier this week.
Analysts said Tatneft would develop the prize field and use the output to pay off federal taxes.
Tatneft has said it plans to shed a massive 35 to 40 percent of its total workforce of 75,000 workers, saying it will get rid of those not directly involved in the business of producing oil.

"But I don't expect this to be discussed at tomorrow's shareholders meeting," the Tatneft spokesman said, adding that the main object of the meeting was to vote on a new board and on previously-announced plans of a share split and dividends.
Tatneft announced plans last month for a 100-to-one share split to increase liquidity. It also said it would increase dividends on both ordinary and preferred shares.
Tatneft American Depositary Receipts are listed in Berlin TATN_y.BE.
